[Verified 2026-03-17 | J Surg Res 2017 | content_match] The Association for Academic Surgery was founded in 1966 with 33 members. Zuidema was the founding member and first president (1968). The AAS mission was to offer young academic surgeons an inclusive forum for discussion about surgical research and professional growth, with active membership lasting 12 years after first academic appointment. Patricia Joy Numann (b. 1941), endocrine surgeon at SUNY Upstate Medical University, founded the Association of Women Surgeons (AWS) in 1981 by inviting as many female surgeons as she could identify to a breakfast at the October ACS Clinical Congress in San Francisco. At that time, there was no formal organization serving the needs of women surgeons. Numann served as AWS president (1986-1987) and the organization has since grown into a national society supporting women medical students, residents, and surgeons. Numann was also the first woman to chair the American Board of Surgery (1994-2002), the first woman second vice-president of the ACS (1999-2000), and the second woman president of the ACS (2011, 92nd president, after Kathryn Anderson). She received the ACS Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019, only the fourth surgeon so honored. The founding of AWS parallels the generational society pattern in the graph — a new organization emerging because the existing structures (ACS, ASA, SUS) did not adequately serve a constituency — in this case, women surgeons. The Nina Starr Braunwald Award of the AWS (which Numann received in 1998) is named after Nina Starr Braunwald, who is already a node in the graph, creating a cultural connection between these two women in surgery edges.

target_node: Johns Hopkins Hospital Department of Surgery
notes: route: 12_governance_societies Dean DeWitt Lewis succeeded William Stewart Halsted as professor of surgery and surgeon-in-chief at Johns Hopkins, serving until his retirement in 1939. He is the second of the department's chairs and closes the post-Halsted leadership gap between Halsted (d. September 1922) and Alfred Blalock (from 1941). Governance bar satisfied: documented surgeon-in-chief / professor-of-surgery appointment, not an administrative dean/VC title. Corroborating locator: the Johns Hopkins Department of Surgery history page, which names the post-Halsted chair succession as Lewis, Blalock, Zuidema, Cameron, Freischlag, Higgins. Independent corroboration: Hoopes JE, 'Letter from America: Hopkins reunion,' J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg (S1748-6815(09)00803-1), which names the first three chairmen of surgery at Hopkins as Halsted, Dean Lewis and Alfred Blalock. Tenure dates verified 2026-07-25 against the Alan Mason Chesney Medical Archives portrait record for Dean DeWitt Lewis (the evidence_locator), which states that Johns Hopkins recruited Lewis to succeed William S. Halsted as professor of surgery and surgeon-in-chief and that he held the post until his retirement in 1939; the 1925 start is consistent with the record's account of his 1925 departure from Rush. No upstream training edge is authored: Lewis took his MD at Rush (1899) and studied anatomy at Leipzig under Spalteholz, an anatomist rather than a surgical program director, so no endpoint satisfies the direct_training bar. Lewis therefore enters the person-to-person lineage projection as a trunk root.
